part2.intro: Three young people talk about their jobs on the school magazine.
part2.question: For each question, choose the correct answer.

texts.label: A
texts.title: Priya
texts.text: I write the sports page for our school magazine. Every week I watch the school teams play and write an article about the match. My grandfather was a sports writer for a newspaper, and he gives me lots of tips. Last month the town council gave me a diploma for my article about our girls' football team! I'd love to work for a big newspaper one day.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Jonas
texts.text: My job is the advertisements. The magazine costs a lot to print, so I visit shops and cafés in our town and ask them to pay for an advert. It isn't easy – some owners say no – but I've already found twelve. One café near the school even gave us its menu to put in the magazine. I'm not very good at writing, but I'm good at talking to people!

texts.label: C
texts.title: Hoa
texts.text: I answer the letters on the 'Ask Hoa' page. Students write to me about their problems – friends, homework or parents – and I write back with advice. I never print their names. I wasn't sure about the job at first, but my English teacher said I'd be good at it. Sometimes I get twenty letters a week, so I write my answers in a notebook on the bus.

items.q: Who gets advice from an older relative?
Who brings money to the magazine?
Who keeps some people's names secret?
Who has received a prize for their writing?
Who says one part of their job is difficult?
Who does some of their work while travelling?
Who has a plan for a future job?

part3.title: A diary from the past
part3.text:
When thirteen-year-old Isla Bennett helped her grandmother clean the attic last spring, she found an old wooden box. Inside, there was a diary, some letters, an old passport and a pile of postcards from the 1960s. They belonged to Isla's great-aunt Margaret, who died before Isla was born.

"At first I just wanted to look at the postcards, because they had beautiful pictures of the seaside," says Isla. "But then I opened the diary and I couldn't stop reading." Margaret wrote it when she was fifteen. In it, she described her school, her friends and her dream of becoming a nurse.

Isla's history teacher, Mr Okoye, was looking for ideas for a class project about life in the past. When Isla showed him the diary, he was very excited. The whole class read parts of it and compared Margaret's school days with their own. "We couldn't believe there were fifty students in her class!" Isla laughs.

Later, a journalist from the local newspaper heard about the project and wrote an article about it. Lots of people in the town read it, and one woman, now eighty, wrote a letter to Isla. She was in Margaret's class at school! She sent Isla a photo of the two girls when they were fifteen.

Now Isla writes in her own diary every evening. "Maybe one day someone will find it in an attic," she says. "I'd like them to know what life was like for me."

items.q: What did Isla want to look at first?
What do we learn about Margaret's diary?
options: She wrote it when she was a teenager.
She wrote it when she was working as a nurse.
She wrote it for a school project.

items.q: What surprised Isla's class?
options: Margaret's school was far from her home.

items.q: What happened after the newspaper article?
options: Isla wrote letters to old people in the town.
Someone who knew Margaret contacted Isla.

items.q: Why does Isla write a diary now?
options: She wants to make it into a book.
She wants people in the future to know about her life.

part4.title: The story of the postcard
part4.text:
The first postcards were {19} in Austria in 1869. They were cheaper to send than letters because people didn't need an envelope. At first, postcards had no pictures. There was only space for an address on one side and a short message on the {20}.

Picture postcards became very popular at the beginning of the twentieth century. People bought them when they went on holiday and sent them to friends and family {21} home. Some people also started to {22} postcards as a hobby and kept them in special books.

Today, most people send emails and text messages instead, so fewer postcards are sent every year. But many people still love getting one, because it shows that someone {23} about them while they were away. And collecting old postcards is still popular – some rare ones {24} hundreds of pounds!

part7.model: Last week Hugo wrote a birthday card for his grandma and posted it. Three days later, the postman brought the card back to Hugo's house. Hugo forgot to put a stamp on the envelope! The card was too late, so he called his grandma and sang 'Happy Birthday' on the phone.

items.q: What did the girl forget to bring to school?

script.t: Oh no, I've left something at home.
Your diary? Mr Green's checking them today.
No, my diary's in my bag. And I've got my library card, too.
So what is it?
The form for the museum trip. Mum signed it last night, but it's still on the kitchen table!

items.q: Which magazine does the boy buy?

script.t: Are you getting your football magazine again?
I usually do, but it's more expensive this month.
What about the games one?
My brother's already bought that, so I can read his. I'll get this one about animals. There's an article about sharks in it.

items.q: How much is the bill?

script.t: Excuse me, I think there's a mistake on our bill. It says thirty pounds.
Let me see. Two pizzas – that's eighteen pounds – and two juices.
Yes, but it also says two ice creams. We didn't have any.
Oh, I'm sorry. So it's twenty-four pounds, not thirty. I'll bring you a new bill.

items.q: Where will the girl put the note for her brother?

script.t: Dad, I'm going to Anna's. I'll leave a note for Sam on the front door.
He always comes in through the garden. Put it on the fridge. He goes there first.
There are too many notes on the fridge already. He won't see it.
Then put it on his bed. He always throws his school bag there when he gets home.
Good idea.

items.q: What is the girl's history project going to be about?

script.t: Have you chosen a topic for your history project?
I wanted to do castles, but Lucy's already doing that.
What about ships? You love the sea.
There aren't any good books about ships in the library. I'll do trains. My grandad's got a box of old train tickets, and I can put them in my project.

part2.intro: You will hear a woman from a local newspaper talking to students about a writing competition.
part2.title: Young Reporters Competition

items.label: Write an article about an interesting:
Name of the newspaper: The … News
The winner gets a diploma and a:
Day the winning article will be in the newspaper:

script.t: Hello, everyone. My name's Helen Shaw, and I work for our local newspaper. I'm here to tell you about our Young Reporters competition. This year, we'd like you to write an article about an interesting person in your town. Last year the topic was buildings, and we got lots of articles about the castle, so we wanted something different! It could be a neighbour, a shop owner or even someone in your family. Your article must be no longer than two hundred and fifty words. Some students sent us five hundred words last year, and we couldn't read them all! You can type it or write it by hand, and send it to us by email or by post. Our newspaper is called The Kesworth News. That's K-E-S-W-O-R-T-H. You'll find our address on the back page. The winner will get a diploma and a new laptop. Last year's winner got a camera, but we think a laptop is more useful for a young reporter. We'll print the winning article in the newspaper on Saturday the twentieth of June. The newspaper usually comes out on Thursdays, but that week we're making a special weekend newspaper. Good luck, everyone!

part3.intro: You will hear Nina talking to her friend Leo about a letter from her favourite writer.

items.q: How did Nina contact the writer?
What did the writer send Nina?
How long did Nina wait for an answer?
What was the writer's advice?
options: write in a diary every day

items.q: What is Nina going to do this weekend?
options: write an article for the school magazine
send another letter to the writer

script.t: Hi Nina. You look happy!
I am! Do you remember I wanted to write to Ruby Hart, the writer of the Moon Island books?
Yes. Did you send her an email?

I wanted to, but there was no email address on her website. So I wrote her a real letter and sent it to the company that makes her books. I put a birthday card in the envelope too, because it was her birthday that month.
Nice. When did you send it?
In September, so I waited two months. I thought she'd never answer. Then yesterday a big envelope arrived.
What was in it? A signed book?
I hoped so! But no, it was a long letter, and at the bottom she drew a picture of the dragon from Moon Island. It's amazing. I'm going to put it on my bedroom wall.
Cool. What did she say?
I asked her how to become a writer. She said lots of people tell you to read a lot, and that's important, but the best thing is to write in a diary every day – even just a few lines.
Are you going to do that?
I've already started! And Mr Davis wants me to write an article about the letter for the school magazine. I'm doing that this weekend.
Maybe one day you'll write your own book!
Maybe – but not yet!

items.intro: You will hear a boy talking to his mother about a form.
items.q: What does the boy need help with?

script.t: Mum, can you help me with this form for the swimming club? I've already written my name and address.
So what's the problem? I've paid for it already.
It asks for the name and phone number of our doctor. I don't know them.
OK, I'll find them for you after dinner.

items.intro: You will hear a girl talking about a newspaper article.
items.q: Why did she like the article?
options: It was about someone she knows.

script.t: Did you see the article in yesterday's newspaper about the old cinema? The photos were OK, but the best part was the interview with Mr Brooks. He lives next door to us! He told them about working at the cinema fifty years ago. I'm going to cut it out and keep it.

items.intro: You will hear a man talking to a waitress in a café.
items.q: What is the problem?
options: The menu is not in English.

script.t: Excuse me. I don't think this bill is mine. I only had a cheese sandwich and a coffee, but this says two burgers and a milkshake.
Oh, I'm so sorry. That's for the table by the window. Here's yours.
Thank you. And the sandwich was lovely.

items.intro: You will hear a teacher talking to her class about their projects.
items.q: What is the teacher doing?
options: telling students what their projects must have

script.t: Remember, your projects about famous people are due on Friday. Every project must have at least three pictures and a list of the books and websites you used. If it doesn't have these, I can't give you a good mark. No, Tom, I'm sorry, I can't give you more time. Friday is the last day.

items.intro: You will hear two friends talking about a magazine.
items.q: What does the girl think about the magazine now?
options: It isn't as interesting as before.

script.t: Are you still buying Pop Teen every week?
No, I stopped last month. It's the same price as before, and there aren't more adverts than in other magazines. But all the articles are about the same three singers now. It's boring.
Oh, I didn't know that.

part5.intro: You will hear Tom talking to his mum about the post. What did each person get?

script.t: Mum, the post's here! There's lots today.
Great. Is there anything for me? I'm waiting for my new driving licence.
Yes, this one's for you. It says 'Driving Licence' on the envelope.
Finally! Now I can drive again. What else?
This one's for Dad. It looks like a bill.
Oh dear. It's probably the phone bill. He won't be happy.
And here's a postcard for Grandma. It's got a picture of Rome on it.
That's from her friend Maria. She's on holiday in Italy. Is there a birthday card for Grandma, too? It's her birthday next week.
No, nothing else for Grandma. Here's Lucy's magazine – the one about horses. She gets it every month.
She'll be pleased. Anything from school? They said they'd send a letter about the trip.
No, nothing from school. And the newspaper isn't here yet.
It always comes later on Saturdays.
Oh, and look – this one's for me! It's my ticket for the concert in May!
Lucky you! Is that everything?
There's just an advertisement for a new pizza restaurant. Shall I put it in the bin?
